data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference is defensible through a 'betting quotient' model where corroboration functions not as probability but as a measure of risk exposure; preferring the corroborated theory is simply minimizing the known risk of immediate falsification, not maximizing the chance of future truth.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If avoiding known falsehoods implicitly assumes that the remaining options are safer, which is an inductive jump.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'risk' in this context cannot be defined without reference to future outcomes (probabilities).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'unknown risk' of the corroborated theory is effectively treated as lower than the 'known risk' of the falsified one via an implicit inductive weighting.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Risk-Minimization Heuristic: This mechanism treats scientific action as a series of bets. A falsified theory has a risk of 1.0 (it is known wrong). A corroborated theory has an unknown risk. Rational agency dictates minimizing known risks. Therefore, preferring the corroborated theory is a deduction from the axiom 'avoid known falsehoods,' requiring no inductive assumption about the future success of the chosen theory, only the logical avoidance of the refuted ones.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
